findings.message: CONFIRMED (🟠). `toCheckpointObjectKey` in `/home/afgan0r/Projects/SolidGames/replays-fetcher/src/checkpoint/object-key.ts` raises raw `new Error(...)` on all three validation failures — empty prefix (line 43), empty post-sanitization slug (line 48), and non-S3-safe key (lines 53-55) — instead of a typed `AppError` subclass. This file sits in the Capability band (`src/checkpoint/**`), whose role per the layer map is exactly "returns validated domain data, raises typed errors"; it is neither the composition root nor the CLI entrypoint, so it is in `typed-errors-only` scope. These are NOT the rule's exempt "internal programmer-guard / assertion" throws: the file's own header documents them as a security boundary (threat T-09-05), the `prefix` is operator-controlled config and the `slug` derives from the external source URL, and the store invokes this on the live ingest write path at `src/checkpoint/s3-checkpoint-store.ts:151` and `:169` right before a PutObject/GetObject. They are input-validation failures on externally-influenced data — precisely what should raise an `AppError`. The repo already has the machinery (`src/errors/app-error.ts`, plus subclasses `CheckpointConflictError`, `ReplayByteFetchError`, `SourceFetchError`). SCOPE CORRECTION for the downstream agent: this is a class defect, not one line — the identical anti-pattern lives in the two sibling Capability key-builders and must be fixed together: `src/evidence/object-key.ts:35,40,45` (runId/prefix, threat T-11-01) and `src/storage/object-key.ts:5` (checksum guard). The raw throws in `src/commands/*.ts` (Command/composition band) and the inner `throw new Error("Expected boolean-like value")` in `src/config.ts:26` (a Zod-transform guard re-typed by the surrounding `ConfigValidationError`) are correctly OUT of scope — do not touch them.
findings.fix: Add one typed error in `src/errors/` following the `CheckpointConflictError` template — a concrete `class ObjectKeyValidationError extends AppError<"object-key-invalid">` with an identifiers-only `details` payload (e.g. `{ reason: "empty-prefix" | "empty-slug" | "unsafe-key" }`, never the raw prefix/slug bytes per the app-error.ts threat note) and an explicit `this.name = "ObjectKeyValidationError"`. Replace the three raw `throw new Error(...)` in `src/checkpoint/object-key.ts` (lines 43, 48, 53-55) with `throw new ObjectKeyValidationError({ reason: ... })`, and apply the same replacement to the sibling key-builders `src/evidence/object-key.ts:35,40,45` and `src/storage/object-key.ts:5`. Update each file's header comment ("...throws `Error` on invalid input") to name the typed error, and update the existing `.toThrow(...)` assertions in `object-key.test.ts` for all three to assert the typed error/code.

findings.message: Confirmed real violation of `graceful-shutdown` on live code. `createStoreRawResources` (src/commands/shared.ts:212-245) opens two long-lived composition-root clients per invocation — a `pg.Pool` (shared.ts:207-209 via `createStagingRepository`→`createPgPool`) and an `S3Client` (shared.ts:219) — and run-once.ts:104-108 consumes them but never closes either. The returned `StoreRawResources` contract (shared.ts:86-93) and the `StagingRepository` contract (src/staging/stage-raw-replay.ts:7-9) expose no end/close/dispose method, so the action handler has no handle to release them; after `dependencies.runOnce(...)` resolves it only does `writeJson` + `await flushLogger` + sets `process.exitCode` — no `pool.end()`/S3 teardown. The rule is explicit: "A resource opened at composition root that is never closed is a violation." This is not a pre-refactor gap: src/commands/check.ts:25 already ends its pool in a `finally` ("always releases it … [std: correctness §AB] resource lifecycle"), so the standard is live and the ingest commands simply omit it. The Haiku verdict is correct but under-scoped twice: (1) it names only the pg.Pool — the S3Client (shared.ts:219) is leaked identically; (2) the worse instance is src/commands/watch.ts — the actual always-on daemon: it wires the SIGTERM/SIGINT seam (`createShutdownSeam`, watch.ts:40-59) and signals the loop to stop (legs 1+2 of the rule satisfied), but its `finally` (watch.ts:132-138) only `dispose()`s the signal listeners and still never ends the pool or destroys the S3 client (leg 3 — "pg pools and S3 clients are explicitly closed/ended after the loop resolves" — fails). Severity 🟠 per the catalog: a connection/socket leak drained only by OS process exit and server-side idle timeout (unclean drain), not data loss — so not 🔴.
findings.fix: Give the composition root an explicit teardown and call it in a `finally`, mirroring check.ts. In src/commands/shared.ts, have `createStoreRawResources` also return a disposer that closes both clients — capture the `s3Client` and the staging `pool`, and return e.g. `close: async () => { await pool?.end(); s3Client.destroy(); }` on `StoreRawResources` (add it to the interface at shared.ts:86-93; `createStagingRepository` must surface the pool so it can be ended). Then in BOTH command handlers wrap the run in try/finally and await teardown after the pino flush: src/commands/run-once.ts — after `await flushLogger(rootLogger)` / setting `process.exitCode`, `await resources.close()` in a `finally`; src/commands/watch.ts — add `await resources.close()` to the existing `finally` (watch.ts:132-138) alongside `dispose()`. Do not have an adapter close its own client (composition-root fence); the close must live in the command band that built them. Treat this as a class fix across run-once.ts + watch.ts covering both the pg.Pool and the S3Client, not a one-line patch to run-once's pool alone.

findings.message: CONFIRMED. `/home/afgan0r/Projects/SolidGames/replays-fetcher/src/config.ts:5` imports `type { SourceTransport }` from `./discovery/types.js`. Per the layer map, `src/config.ts` is the **CrossCutting** band (listed explicitly in its `dirs`) and `src/discovery/**` is the **Capability** band. CrossCutting declares `mayDependOn: []` with the fence "Cross-cutting modules import only node builtins and npm packages — never any band above them." This import goes CrossCutting → Capability, i.e. upward — a direct fence violation. The import is live, not stale: `SourceTransport` is used at config.ts:193, :198, :218 (it types the `sourceTransport` config field and the `sourceTransportOrUndefined` helper). The code is committed and clean (`git status` empty), so this is live code, not in-flight churn. This is the exact sub-case `band-wrong-placement`'s howToDetect names: "a type shared across bands living in a single band's directory rather than src/types/." `SourceTransport` is shared across bands (config.ts/CrossCutting + discovery/types.ts/Capability, and transitively the orchestration/diagnostics consumers) yet lives in a single band's dir. It also creates a band-level dependency cycle: `discovery/source-client.ts:20` imports `SourceConfig` downward from `../config.js` while `config.ts` imports `SourceTransport` upward from discovery — exactly the coupling `src/types/` exists to break. Severity 🟠 is correct (catalog severity for the rule, architecture:true); not downgraded — this is a refactor-milestone audit where import-direction findings are first-class, and "predates the refactor" is not grounds to overturn (it IS the finding). Note for the milestone: `src/types/run-summary.ts` (also CrossCutting) has the same upward import from `discovery/types.js`, so this is one instance of a small class — but THIS finding is scoped correctly to config.ts:5 and stands on its own.
findings.fix: Extract the cross-band leaf type into the CrossCutting types dir and re-point both consumers — do NOT move the whole `discovery/types.ts` file (it legitimately holds Capability-local types like `DiscoveryReport`, `DiscoveryDiagnostic`, `ReplayCandidate`). Concretely: (1) create `/home/afgan0r/Projects/SolidGames/replays-fetcher/src/types/source-transport.ts` containing `export type SourceTransport = "direct" | "ssh";` (zero dependencies, a pure config enum); (2) in `src/config.ts:5` change the import to `import type { SourceTransport } from "./types/source-transport.js";`; (3) in `src/discovery/types.ts:16` replace the local declaration with a re-export `export type { SourceTransport } from "../types/source-transport.js";` so existing Capability/Orchestration/Diagnostics consumers keep their import path. This removes the CrossCutting→Capability edge and the config↔discovery cycle while preserving every downstream import site. Optionally fold the identical fix for `src/types/run-summary.ts` into the same milestone change, since it shares the defect.

findings.message: CONFIRMED, severity raised 🟡→🟠. `src/config.ts:26` throws a raw `Error("Expected boolean-like value")` from the `booleanFromEnvironment` Zod `.transform()`. This is not a stylistic taxonomy nit — it is a live correctness defect. Per the official Zod v4 docs ("Transform functions should never throw. Thrown errors are not caught by Zod"), a raw throw inside a `.transform()` is NOT converted into a Zod issue and is NOT caught by `safeParse`. It escapes `loadConfig`/`loadSourceConfig` as an untyped raw `Error`, bypassing the `ConfigValidationError` wrapper (config.ts:258-264) entirely. The repo's own test proves this empirically: `src/config.test.ts:312-315` asserts the throw surfaces the raw `"Expected boolean-like value"` string, NOT the `ConfigValidationError` "Invalid configuration: …" message. The transform is wired to two real, reachable config fields — `s3.forcePathStyle` (config.ts:143, env `S3_FORCE_PATH_STYLE`) and `s3.conditionalWrites` (config.ts:154, env `S3_CHECKPOINT_CONDITIONAL_WRITES`) — so a normal operator misconfiguration (`S3_FORCE_PATH_STYLE=maybe`) crashes with a raw `Error` instead of the convention's exit-code-2 typed-error semantics. This both violates `typed-errors-only` (raw Error on the ingest/boot path, not a programmer-guard) and breaks the §C guarantee "a raw `ZodError`/error never escapes to the operator." Distinguish from the genuinely-exempt sibling throws (commands/*.ts "Expected staging repository", postgres-staging-repository.ts:47, the object-key.ts guards): those are internal invariants on data the program itself produced — correct programmer-guards. This one validates EXTERNAL operator input and the raw error reaches the operator, which is exactly what the rule and §C forbid. NOT overturned on "predates refactor" grounds.
findings.fix: Convert the transform to report via Zod's issue channel instead of throwing, so `safeParse` catches it and `loadConfig` wraps it in `ConfigValidationError` (exit code 2). Change the `.transform((value) => {...})` to `.transform((value, ctx) => {...})` and replace `throw new Error("Expected boolean-like value")` with `ctx.addIssue({ code: "custom", message: "Expected boolean-like value (1/true/yes/y or 0/false/no/n)" }); return z.NEVER;`. (In Zod 4 `ctx.addIssue` remains available; `ctx.issues.push({...})` + `return z.NEVER` is the equivalent newer form.) Then update the now-incorrect test expectation at src/config.test.ts:312-315: it must assert the failure surfaces as a `ConfigValidationError` (message beginning "Invalid configuration:" / `.issues` containing the boolean-like message), NOT the bare `"Expected boolean-like value"` string — the current test is asserting the bug. Apply the same `ctx.addIssue`+`z.NEVER` pattern to any other config-schema transform that throws.

findings.message: Confirmed live architecture violation of §A convergence #5 (cross-band data contracts live in cross-cutting `types/`). `RawReplayStorageEvidence` is defined in a single Capability band's dir (`src/storage/types.ts:26`) yet is a contract shared across bands: it is produced by `storage/` (`store-raw-replay.ts:22`, `StoreRawReplayResult = ... | RawReplayStorageEvidence`) and consumed by a *sibling* Capability `staging/` (`payload.ts:8` — the flagged line — plus `staging/types.ts:1`, `staging/stage-raw-replay.ts:5`), with `run/no-leak.test.ts:33` referencing it too. A type needed by more than one band must live in `src/types/`, exactly as §A.5 prescribes for `RunSummary`. Note one correction to the candidate finding's rationale: `payload.ts:8` is *not* itself an upward import — both `storage/` and `staging/` are Capability band, so this is a sibling-to-sibling type import, not a lower-band reaching up into `run/`. The violation is the type's *placement* in a single band's dir, not the import direction on this line; the line is simply a valid witness of the misplaced shared contract. This is precisely the kind of layer-placement debt the refactor milestone targets, and "it predates the refactor" is not a defense — §A.5 names this same pattern as live debt.
findings.fix: Relocate the shared raw-storage contract from `src/storage/types.ts` into cross-cutting `src/types/` (e.g. a new `src/types/raw-replay-evidence.ts`), moving the cluster `RawReplayStorageEvidence` together with the types it composes — `RawReplayObjectIdentity` and `RawReplayStorageStatus` — since they travel with it across bands. Re-point every importer to the new path: `storage/{s3-raw-storage,store-raw-replay,types}.ts`, `staging/{payload,types,stage-raw-replay}.ts`, and the affected test files. Per §A.5, the *type* moves to `types/` while the *builders* stay in their owning bands — `s3-raw-storage.ts` (which constructs the evidence) remains in `storage/`, and `payload.ts` remains in `staging/`. After the move, `staging/payload.ts:8` imports the contract from `../types/...` (cross-cutting, downward) instead of from a sibling Capability dir. Keep `StageableRawReplayEvidence` (the `staging/`-local narrowing) in `staging/types.ts` — it is staging-specific, not cross-band.

Per the fetcher conventions §A band table and Convergence rule 5, "a type shared by more than one band lives in `types/`, not in [its producing band]" — with `RunSummary` given as the worked example of exactly this. `ReplayCandidate` is that case: produced by `discovery/`, consumed by `storage/` (`store-raw-replay.ts`, `s3-raw-storage.ts`, `storage/types.ts`), by `run/` (`ingest-page.ts`, `run-once.ts`, `watch-loop.ts`), AND — the load-bearing proof — by the Cross-cutting band itself at `src/types/run-summary.ts:4`, where `RunSummary.candidates: readonly ReplayCandidate[]` forces `types/` to import UPWARD into the `discovery/` Capability. That upward import is the identical layer violation rule 5 names for the pre-move `evidence/`→`run/` case, so this is genuine misplacement, not a same-tier-import quibble. The "code predates the refactor" angle does not excuse it — that gap is the finding. Severity 🟠 is correct (rule catalog severity; architecture/import-direction finding driving the refactor milestone). Note: the Haiku verdict's reasoning is right but it flagged a weak instance — `store-raw-replay.ts` is a Capability importing a sibling Capability's type (same tier), whereas the strongest evidence of the defect is the upward import at `src/types/run-summary.ts:4`. The named span is still a true symptom and stays verified.
findings.fix: Relocate the TYPE, do not patch this single import. Move the `ReplayCandidate` interface (and any tightly-coupled discovery payload types it composes — `DiscoveryDiagnostic`, `DiagnosticCode`, `DiscoveryReport` are co-imported by `types/run-summary.ts`) from `src/discovery/types.ts` into a cross-cutting `src/types/` module (e.g. `src/types/discovery.ts` or a shared `src/types/candidate.ts`). Per §A, the type moves but the BUILDER stays: `discovery/discover.ts` keeps constructing `ReplayCandidate` (it now imports the type downward from `types/`). Then repoint all ~8 importers to the new path — `storage/store-raw-replay.ts:9`, `storage/s3-raw-storage.ts:11`, `storage/types.ts:1`, `run/ingest-page.ts:2`, `run/run-once.ts:25`, `run/watch-loop.ts:10`, `discovery/discover.ts:8`, and critically `types/run-summary.ts:4` (which then imports a sibling `types/` module instead of reaching up into `discovery/`). After the move, re-run the depcruise/fence check: `types/` must import nothing from `discovery/`. Fixing only `store-raw-replay.ts:9` in isolation is wrong — it leaves the type in the wrong band and leaves the `types/run-summary.ts` upward import intact.

findings.message: band-wrong-placement confirmed: `ReplayCandidate` is a cross-band data contract but is defined inside the `discovery/` Capability band (`src/discovery/types.ts:18`). It is consumed across three bands — Capability `src/storage/{types,s3-raw-storage,store-raw-replay}.ts`, Orchestration `src/run/{ingest-page,run-once,watch-loop}.ts`, and, decisively, the CrossCutting types band `src/types/run-summary.ts:4`. Per §A convergence adjustment 5 ("A type shared by more than one band ... lives in cross-cutting `types/`, not in a single band's dir"), it is misplaced. This is the identical defect already acknowledged in the skill for `RunSummary` (the named example in adjustment 5), generalized to `ReplayCandidate`. The live proof is an inverted import: `src/types/run-summary.ts` — whose CrossCutting fence is explicitly "imports nothing upward / only node builtins and npm packages, never any band above" — currently imports `ReplayCandidate`, `DiagnosticCode`, and `DiscoveryDiagnostic` UP from `../discovery/types.js`. So the defect is not cosmetic filing; it forces a real upward dependency from the lowest band. Note on the quoted anchor: the finding pins `src/storage/types.ts:1` (storage → discovery, which is sideways Capability-to-Capability, not itself the upward violation). The true violation is the misplaced *definition* in `discovery/types.ts`; `storage/types.ts:1` and `types/run-summary.ts:4` are two of its consumers. The finding's rule (file/type living in the wrong band) and its named remedy (move to `src/types/`) are correct, so it stands — but the fix below retargets the definition, not just that one import line. Verified safe to move: `src/discovery/types.ts` has no back-import from `../types`, so relocation introduces no import cycle.
findings.fix: Move the cross-band discovery contracts UP into the CrossCutting types band, then repoint consumers — do not just edit `storage/types.ts:1`. Concretely: (1) Relocate `ReplayCandidate`, and the diagnostic types that travel with it across bands (`DiagnosticCode`, `DiscoveryDiagnostic`, `DiagnosticSeverity`), from `src/discovery/types.ts` into `src/types/` (e.g. a new `src/types/replay-candidate.ts` or extend the existing `src/types/` module set). (3) Keep all builders/producers in their owning bands — discovery still constructs `ReplayCandidate` values; only the type definition relocates, mirroring how `RunSummary`'s builder stays in `run/summary.ts`. (4) Run `tsc --noEmit` to confirm no cycle and no missed import.

findings.message: CONFIRMED, severity corrected 🟠→🟡. `src/commands/clients.ts:24-25` — `createPgPool` constructs `new Pool({ connectionString: databaseUrl })` with no explicit limits or timeouts (`max`, `connectionTimeoutMillis`, `idleTimeoutMillis`, `statement_timeout`/`query_timeout`). A pool with no `connectionTimeoutMillis` blocks indefinitely when Postgres is unreachable, and no `max` lets concurrent ingest exhaust server connections — exactly the unbounded-wait / resource-exhaustion the rule guards. This is the live state of the code, not a pre-refactor artifact. Haiku correctly verified the violation but over-leveled it to 🟠; the catalog pins `long-lived-client-configured` at 🟡 and there is no gate-level (data-loss/security) escalation here — it is resilience hardening, so the rule severity governs. NOTE for the downstream agent: the SAME rule defect exists one function up at `createS3Client` (lines 13-22) — no `requestHandler` timeout and no `maxAttempts` retry cap — and should be fixed in the same pass (the rule title names pg.Pool AND S3Client).

For the pool: `new Pool({ connectionString: databaseUrl, max: 10, connectionTimeoutMillis: 5000, idleTimeoutMillis: 30000, statement_timeout: 30000 })` (tune values to the ingest concurrency cap). For the S3 client, pass a `requestHandler` with connection/socket timeouts (e.g. `new NodeHttpHandler({ connectionTimeout: 5000, requestTimeout: 30000 })` from `@smithy/node-http-handler`) and an explicit `maxAttempts` retry cap. findings.message: Real violation of `test-parameterized-tables`, but the severity is wrong. `src/source/classify-failure.test.ts:93-104` ("classifyFailure should classify network cause codes as transient") is an input matrix — `["ECONNRESET","ENOTFOUND","EAI_AGAIN","ETIMEDOUT"]` — driven through one identical `expect(classifyFailure({ error })).toMatchObject({ causeCode: code, kind: "transient" })` per iteration via a manual `for…of`. That is exactly the pattern the rule says to collapse into `test.each([...])`; a hand-rolled loop is the same anti-pattern in different syntax (on failure it reports no per-input case name and short-circuits on the first bad code, hiding the rest). The repo already standardizes on this idiom (`src/config.test.ts:131,149,169,187,442,460`; `src/contract-check/contract-check.test.ts:218,238`), so the loop is off-convention here. The finding is correct, but Haiku graded it 🟠; the active catalog fixes this ruleId at 🔵 and there is no escalation basis — it is test ergonomics, not a correctness/architecture defect. Corrected severity: 🔵. This is a class, not a one-off: the identical `for…of` + single-`toMatchObject` shape recurs at lines 31-43, 45-52, 54-67, 119-134, and 136-144 of the same file; fix them in the same pass.
findings.fix: Convert the loop to `test.each` so each input is its own named case. Match the repo idiom: either inline (`test.each(["ECONNRESET","ENOTFOUND","EAI_AGAIN","ETIMEDOUT"])("classifyFailure should classify network cause code %s as transient", (code) => { const error = Object.assign(new TypeError("fetch failed"), { cause: Object.assign(new Error("transport"), { code }) }); expect(classifyFailure({ error })).toMatchObject({ causeCode: code, kind: "transient" }); });`) or, to mirror config.test.ts, hoist a `readonly (readonly [string])[]` cases array and pass it to `test.each`. Apply the same transform to the sibling loops at lines 31-43 (5xx → transient), 45-52 (408/425 → transient), 54-67 (4xx/404/410 → permanent), 119-134 (TLS codes), and 136-144 (AbortError/TimeoutError), preserving each test's `(...)` title suffix (e.g. WR-02, F2) via a `%s` placeholder.

findings.message: Cross-band coupling on a shared utility, but the finding targets the wrong file and over-applies the rule. `src/staging/payload.ts:1` imports `calculateSha256` from `../storage/checksum.js`. The genuine smell is that `calculateSha256` (src/storage/checksum.ts — a 2-line generic `createHash("sha256")…` wrapper, zero storage-specific logic) is a cross-cutting helper now consumed by TWO sibling Capability bands — `storage/store-raw-replay.ts` and `staging/payload.ts` — yet it is owned by one capability's directory. The layer-map CrossCutting band is where anything shared across bands belongs; a generic crypto helper living under `storage/` and reached sideways by `staging/` is the architectural issue. HOWEVER the finding is mis-filed: (1) `band-wrong-placement` flags a *file in the wrong band*; `payload.ts` is correctly in `staging/` (building the staging payload IS staging's job) — the only arguably-misplaced file is `storage/checksum.ts`, not `payload.ts`; the import line is the symptom, not the violation. (2) The cited rule (§A.5 / catalog `howToDetect`) is scoped to **types / data contracts** ("a *type* shared across bands … rather than src/types/"); Haiku widened it to "types or shared utilities" and proposed `src/source/`, but `source/` is defined as resilience primitives only and §A.5 says nothing about utility *functions*. No catalog rule squarely prohibits a shared utility function's location, so this is an in-spirit placement nit, not the 🟠 cross-band-contract break §A.5 describes (which is the upward `RunSummary` import — this import is downward-adjacent between two capabilities, no layer inversion). Hence verified but down-leveled to 🔵: a tiny pure helper, no behavior/correctness/security impact, low-priority refactor tidy-up.
findings.fix: Retarget to `src/storage/checksum.ts`, not `payload.ts`. During the refactor milestone, lift the generic `calculateSha256` helper out of the `storage/` capability into the CrossCutting band so both `storage/` and `staging/` import it sideways-free. Since `src/source/` is reserved for resilience primitives and `src/types/` is for data contracts, introduce a small cross-cutting utility home (e.g. `src/util/checksum.ts` or `src/crypto/checksum.ts`) under CrossCutting, move `calculateSha256` there, and update the two importers (`storage/store-raw-replay.ts`, `staging/payload.ts`) plus the test. Do NOT relocate `payload.ts` — it is correctly placed. If the team prefers, add an explicit rule/destination for shared utility functions to §A so future findings cite real rule text rather than the types-only §A.5.
